chapter: From Pittsburgh to Maxine Sullivan: management and style
title: Her voice, range and style over the years
summary: Her range is the same but the voice has changed; her light voice was natural for the arrangements of the time.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Has your range changed over the years?
Well, my range is pretty much the same. But there just seems to be a different timbre.

There's a little bit more - before it just sounded like it was floating on nothing. Which I can appreciate because I knew that somewhere as I got older this was the change. And I don't like to do things like "Loch Loman" and "Molly Malone" and "If I Had A Ribbon Bow" / with the kind of a voice I have now because it would sound like I'm really jazzing it up, and I really don't intend to.

What were some of the other elements of your style since, you know, since you're talking about style now? You mentioned to me before that you had to develop a microphone style because you didn't naturally have a very robust voice.

Well, because I didn't have a robust voice, my voice was natural for a microphone with the amplification. And I didn't have to develop a microphone voice. I don't know if I'm allowed to describe what my voice was like in those days. It was mostly breathe. I didn't seem to have that resistance, that bottom that singers usually have. And then after I got involved with those things like "Loch Loman" and "Molly and "If I Had A Ribbon Bow" Malone" / it required that kind of a quality so I think that's what I developed. It really consisted of mostly

high notes. And these would be the highlights, the quality that the arrangers and everyone I was associated with wanted to bring out. And it wasn't exactly what I wanted to do, never was what I wanted to do. I am doing more of what I like to do now because it gives me an opportunity to do more, and sort of, interpret the songs the way I'd like to. You see, in the early days you were supposed to stick to the melody entirely, where now, I mean, if you listen to recordings, singers have more freedom. They can improvise if they know how.
Yeah, so there was a kind of match then between that quality of your voice and the material.
Yeah, Yeah, well, I developed that. I found that I had to.
But when you sang ballots like "My Ideal," "Easy To Love" or "Night and Day", you know, and some of the other songs that you did, you know, you also did those very, very effectively.
It's a very different quality of voice than I have now.
